# Exact finite coupling of corner losses and double-sector growth

This note retains the actual six prescribed ray endpoints of a strict
distinct-vertex triangle. It provides an exact area-feasibility frontier
when at most two unique sectors lose area. It is not a proof of the cubic
inequality beyond the already proved pure-loss regime.

## 1. Triangle blocks and reciprocal area changes

Let T be a triangle with an interior source and three balanced spanning
normals whose caps strictly isolate its three different vertices. Fix its
six ray endpoints. The three double sectors are cores; the three unique
sectors have strictly positive excess. Accordingly its exact sector matrix
L_T consists of three singular two-node blocks, one per unique corner.
This follows either from the actual straight boundary joins or directly
from the exact charge/Gram reconstruction.

In unique block i normalize the positive kernel to (alpha_i,beta_i), with
alpha_i+beta_i=1. There is a positive number lambda_i such that

    L_T,i=lambda_i [[beta_i^2,-alpha_i beta_i],
                   [-alpha_i beta_i,alpha_i^2]].       (1)

Its off-diagonal is strictly negative, so lambda_i>0. These constants are
fixed by the actual triangle and its actual cutting rays. More explicitly,
if its unique vertex is V_i=uP+vQ between its two ray endpoints, then
(alpha_i,beta_i)=(v,u)/(u+v), by the exact sector reconstruction formulas.

Write X_i^T for the unique-sector areas and Y_j^T for the double core areas.
Consider prescribed new sector areas

    core_i<=X_i<=X_i^T,        Y_j>=Y_j^T,

all finite and positive. Define reciprocal changes

    l_i=1/(2X_i)-1/(2X_i^T)>=0,
    g_j=1/(2Y_j^T)-1/(2Y_j)>=0.                        (2)

For a unique edge, reducing area adds l_i 11^T to its two-node block.
For a double edge joining two different unique blocks, increasing area
subtracts g_j aa^T, where a has entry one at those two incident nodes and
zero elsewhere. Hence the full matrix is EXACTLY

    L=blockdiag_i C_i -sum_double j g_j a_j a_j^T,
    C_i=L_T,i+l_i [[1,1],[1,1]].                       (3)

There is no approximation or first-order truncation in (2)--(3).
The original exact PSD theorem says these finite data are realized by an
actual convex body with the prescribed rays if and only if L is PSD.

## 2. A zero corner loss forbids both neighboring double gains

Embed each normalized triangle kernel in its own block, forming three
vectors w_i with disjoint supports. Restrict (3) to their span. The unique
term contributes exactly l_i on diagonal i, because its endpoint weights
sum to one. Each double edge contributes a negative rank-one form whose
two coefficients are the positive kernel entries at its incident nodes.

If l_i=0 and either adjacent g_j>0, evaluation on w_i gives a strictly
negative quadratic form. Therefore actual feasibility forces

    l_i=0  ==> both double gains adjacent to corner i vanish. (4)

In particular, with zero or one positive corner loss, ALL double gains
must vanish: every double edge has an incident unchanged corner. The data
then differ from T only by unique losses and are covered globally by the
cubic loss theorem in
`candidate b59c030c1c2567d0`.

This conclusion uses actual sector feasibility; it would be false for
independently chosen nonnegative raw gains and losses.

## 3. Exact frontier with two changed unique sectors

Suppose exactly two corner losses l_i,l_j are positive, while the third is
zero. By (4), the only possibly positive double gain is their joining edge;
write it as g. Let theta_i be the kernel entry (alpha_i or beta_i) at that
edge's endpoint in block i, and define theta_j similarly.

For l_i>0 the block C_i is positive definite. Indeed its determinant is
lambda_i l_i, since alpha_i+beta_i=1. Its endpoint inverse diagonal is
exactly

    (C_i^{-1})_endpoint,endpoint
       =theta_i^2/l_i+1/lambda_i.                     (5)

For instance at the first node, the numerator in the inverse formula is
lambda_i alpha_i^2+l_i, giving (5); the second node gives beta_i instead.

The four-node part of (3) is blockdiag(C_i,C_j)-g aa^T. Since its block
diagonal is positive definite, conjugation by its square root gives a
rank-one perturbation of the identity. It is PSD if and only if

    g [theta_i^2/l_i+theta_j^2/l_j
                  +1/lambda_i+1/lambda_j] <=1.        (6)

Equivalently, when g>0,

    1/g >=theta_i^2/l_i+theta_j^2/l_j
                       +1/lambda_i+1/lambda_j.         (7)

The unchanged third block is PSD and decoupled. Consequently (6), together
with the finite positive area and core bounds above, is a NECESSARY AND
SUFFICIENT condition for an actual convex-body realization of these data.
It is an exact finite area frontier; no theorem-strength missing geometry
is hidden in the passage from the matrix to a body.

In ordinary areas, let the reciprocal of the bracket in (6) be g_* and
put c_T=1/(2Y^T). Actual finite Y corresponds to 0<=g<c_T. If g_*<c_T,
the exact upper area is

    Y<=Y^T/(1-2Y^T g_*).

If g_*>=c_T there is no finite additional upper bound on Y from (6).
The original cap conditions, if imposed, remain separate actual inequalities.

At g=g_*<c_T the four-node part has rank three, since a nonzero rank-one
subtraction saturates its sole critical eigenvalue. The third two-node
block has rank one. Thus the full matrix has rank four and contains core
edges. The sparse-slack reconstruction theorem provides an actual
quadrilateral with EXACTLY these sector areas and ray endpoints. Possible
additional core equalities in the changed unique sectors do not alter this
rank argument or create an untracked generic-position assumption.

## Scope

The theorem closes pure-loss data and gives a fully actual scalar frontier
for the next coupled two-corner/one-double-edge family. It does not assert
that every quadrilateral lies in that family, that the cubic bound holds
throughout (6), or that any reconstructed body remains compatible with
mixed-integer neighboring fibers.

## 4. Exact quadrilateral incidence reduction

Let K be an actual triangle or quadrilateral containing zero in its interior,
and suppose each of its three balanced through-source cap areas is less
than |K|/2. Use the canonical six rays and unique/double sectors of
`candidate fbdac92a89eef394`.
That theorem supplies the triangle T with the same six ray endpoints,
larger unique sectors, and double sectors equal to their cores.

If an OPEN unique sector contains no vertex of K, its area is exactly its
core area. Indeed the portion of the polygonal boundary between the two
bounding ray endpoints has no vertex in its relative interior: every point
on that boundary arc has an angle strictly between the bounding angles.
The arc is therefore the segment joining those endpoints. Vertices at its
endpoints do not change this conclusion. The intersection with the sector
is the triangle spanned by that segment and zero.

Consequently the case in which some unique sector has no vertex reduces
to an actual UNIQUE-CORE configuration. No cap-ceiling exclusion for that
configuration is asserted here.

Suppose instead all three open unique sectors contain vertices. At least
three distinct vertices are then required. There are only the following
possibilities.

* If no open double sector contains a vertex, all three double sectors
  are cores, by the same boundary-arc argument. The actual data differ
  from T only by unique-sector losses. The global cubic loss theorem
  proves the cubic inequality, strictly unless K=T. This includes a fourth
  vertex in a unique sector or on a cutting ray.
* Otherwise there are precisely four vertices: one in each open unique
  sector, and one in one open double sector. The latter sector has strictly
  positive excess over its core; the other two double sectors are cores.
  The unique corner OPPOSITE the enlarged double sector is unchanged from
  T. Its two neighboring double bridge segments are actual straight
  polygon edges and meet at this corner's sole actual vertex, so their
  intersection is the same vertex of T. The whole unique-sector triangle
  therefore agrees. Both other unique sectors have strictly positive
  losses: otherwise (4) would forbid the adjacent positive double gain.

In the second case T has strict distinct-vertex incidence. Each actual
unique vertex belongs to T's corresponding unique sector, which consequently
has a point strictly beyond its core chord. Its T vertex is thus strictly
inside that open unique cone; a triangle vertex on a bounding ray would
leave that unique sector equal to its core.

Moreover the exact frontier (6) is SATURATED. The six actual ray endpoints
lie in relative interiors of K's four edges, because all four vertices are
in open sectors. Apply the exact reciprocal construction using the actual
vertex in each of the four noncore sectors. Its six ray turns all vanish.
The corresponding positive reconstruction vector therefore satisfies
Lw=0 on every node (equivalently the ray slack formula is
delta_i=(Lw)_i/w_i=0). The unchanged unique sector is its singular two-node
block. The other four nodes form a connected block with positive excess
on its three connecting edges, so its positive kernel makes that block
singular. Conjugating its expression in Section 3 by
blockdiag(C_i,C_j)^(-1/2) proves

    g [theta_i^2/l_i+theta_j^2/l_j
                  +1/lambda_i+1/lambda_j] = 1.       (8)

This argument uses actual straight-edge turns, not an assumption that
every feasible area array has a unique polygonal realization.

Thus, among actual half-cap quadrilaterals, the only remaining possibilities
not settled by the global unique-loss cubic theorem are (i) at least one
unique sector is core, or (ii) a strict-incidence triangle with exactly two
positive unique losses and its one connecting double gain at the exact
rank-four frontier (8). The classification does not exclude either case
by a numerical screen and does not require general position.
